intro.html: Two roots mean time. Greek chron gives us chronic and chronicle; Latin temp or tempor gives us temporary and tempo. A third Latin root, ann or enn, means year, as in annual and anniversary. Spot them, and a whole family of time words opens up.
chron (Greek) = time. temp, tempor (Latin) = time. ann, enn (Latin) = year. Then read the prefix: syn- together, ana- back or against, con- with, ex- out of, per- through.
Each hook below points at the root. Say the parts out loud (syn-CHRON-ize: same time), look at the picture, then check the meaning in the sentences.

words.def: lasting a long time, or coming back again and again
words.ex: Kai is a {chronic} latecomer: he has missed the first bell every day this month.
words.ctx: The leaky faucet was not a one-time problem but a {chronic} one; no matter how often it was fixed, the dripping started again within a week.
words.etym: From Greek chronikos, “having to do with time,” from chronos, “time.”
words.note: Chronic means long-lasting or recurring, not “severe.” A chronic cough may be mild; it just keeps coming back.

mn.cue: CHRON = TIME: trouble that lasts a long TIME
mn.text: The kitchen faucet has dripped every day for a whole year: drip, drip, drip. The leak is {chronic}.

scene.alt: A man scratches his head beside a bucket catching a faucet drip that has gone on for a whole year.

words.def: a record of events in the order they happened
words.ex: Nana Lou keeps a {chronicle} of every family trip in a fat green notebook.
words.ctx: The old ship’s log was a day-by-day {chronicle} of the voyage, recording every storm, every sighting of land and every supper of salted fish.
words.etym: From Greek chronika, “records of the times,” from chronos, “time.”

mn.cue: CHRON-icle: a TIME record, day by day
mn.text: Sami writes down each day of the class trip in order, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, in his travel book: it is a {chronicle} of the trip.

scene.alt: A boy writes in a travel notebook under a banner listing the days of the week in order.

words.def: arranged in the order in which things happened
words.ex: Ivy lined up her baby pictures in {chronological} order, from her first day to her fifth birthday.
words.ctx: The museum’s halls are {chronological}: you begin with ancient stone tools in the first room and finish with rockets and robots in the last.
words.etym: From chronology, from Greek chronos (time) + logos (word, account).

mn.text: Ivy hangs her photos in order of time: baby, toddler, first grade, now. The row is {chronological}.

scene.alt: A girl points to a row of her photos hung in order from age one to now.

words.def: something placed in the wrong time period
words.ex: A knight checking his phone would be a funny {anachronism} in a movie about castles.
words.ctx: The play was set in ancient Rome, so the audience giggled at the {anachronism} when an actor’s wristwatch flashed beneath his toga.
words.etym: From Greek anachronismos: ana (back, against) + chronos (time).

mn.text: A knight in shining armor rolls up to the castle on a skateboard, chatting on his phone. Wrong time! He is an {anachronism}.

scene.alt: A knight in armor rides a skateboard past a castle while talking on a phone.

words.def: to make things happen at the same time or at the same speed
words.ex: Before the race, the timekeepers {synchronized} their stopwatches.
words.ctx: The swimmers {synchronized} every move so perfectly that their legs rose from the water at the very same instant, like parts of a single machine.
words.etym: From Greek synchronos, “happening at the same time”: syn (together) + chronos (time).

mn.text: Three dancers kick their legs at exactly the same moment, on the very same beat: they {synchronize} their moves.

scene.alt: Three dancers on a stage make the very same move at the very same moment.

words.def: living or happening at the same time; also, modern
words.ex: The museum’s new wing shows {contemporary} art, made in the last few years.
words.ctx: Though the two writers never met, they were {contemporary}; both were born in the same year and published their first books within months of each other.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin contemporarius: com (together) + tempus (time).
words.note: Contemporary can mean “of the same time as” (a contemporary of the author) or “modern” (contemporary furniture); context decides.

mn.text: Pip and Kai were born on the very same day and have shared every birthday since: they are {contemporary}, two kids of the same time.

scene.alt: Two boys in party hats cheer beside twin birthday cakes under a banner that says Same Birthday.

words.ex: The story jumps back and forth, so readers must follow its {temporal} clues: dates, seasons and ages.
words.ctx: The detective studied the {temporal} details of the case: what time the lights went out, how long the dog barked and when the car finally drove off.

mn.text: Detective Ada doesn’t ask where the thief went; she asks when. Clock, calendar, timetable: her questions are {temporal}.

scene.alt: A detective with a notebook thinks about when something happened, surrounded by an hourglass, a clock and a calendar.

words.def: spoken or done without any preparation
words.ex: Called on without warning, Dev gave an {extemporaneous} talk about his favorite book.
words.ctx: Most of the toasts had been written weeks ahead, but the best one was {extemporaneous}: the bride’s grandfather simply stood up and spoke from the heart.
words.etym: From Late Latin extemporaneus, from the Latin phrase ex tempore, “out of the moment.”

mn.cue: EX TEMPOR: OUT of the moment
mn.text: Asked to speak with no warning, Grandpa Gus stands right up and talks with no notes at all, straight out of the moment. His speech is {extemporaneous}.

labels.text: EX TEMPORE: NO NOTES, right now

scene.alt: A grandfather speaks into a microphone with no notes while a woman claps.

words.note: Speech teachers use the word more narrowly: a talk planned ahead but given from brief notes, not read or memorized. For no preparation at all, they say impromptu.

words.def: lasting or coming back year after year
words.ex: Pizza is a {perennial} favorite in our school cafeteria.
words.ctx: Weeds are a {perennial} problem in the garden; pull them up in June, and they are back again the next spring.
words.etym: From Latin perennis, “lasting through the years”: per (through) + annus (year).
words.note: Gardeners call a plant that comes back every year a perennial.

mn.text: Every spring, the same red tulips pop up in Nana Lou’s garden, year after year after year: they are {perennial}.

scene.alt: A grandmother kneels happily beside red tulips that bloom again every year.

words.def: a year-by-year record of events; history
words.ex: The great flood is still remembered in the town’s {annals}.
words.ctx: The comeback was the greatest in the {annals} of the school; in a hundred years of yearbooks, no team had ever rallied from so far behind.
words.etym: From Latin annales (libri), “yearly books,” from annus, “year.”
words.note: Annals is nearly always plural: the annals of history.

mn.cue: ANN = YEAR: a book for every YEAR
mn.text: The town library keeps one big book for every year since long ago, shelf after shelf. Together they are the town’s {annals}.

labels.text: ANN-als: a record for each YEAR

scene.alt: An old professor points at big books labeled with years while a teen reads one.

after.html: Two words people stretch. Chronic means long-lasting or coming back again and again, not “very bad”: a chronic problem may be small; it just won’t go away. And contemporary has two senses: “of the same time as” (the painter and her contemporaries) and “modern” (contemporary furniture). Let the sentence decide.

opts.s: The band and the fireworks crew {synchronized} their watches so the music and the first rocket would start at the same moment.
opts.why: Making two things happen at the same time is synchronizing them.

items.q: True or false: a chronic problem is one that is very severe.
items.why: False. Chronic means long-lasting or recurring. A chronic problem may be mild; it just keeps going or coming back.

items.q: In “The painter and her contemporaries often met in the same café,” contemporaries means…
choices: people who lived at the same time as she did
items.why: Here contemporary has its first sense: of the same time. Her contemporaries were people of her own time.

items.q: Which would be an anachronism in a movie about ancient Egypt?
items.why: Wristwatches did not exist in ancient Egypt, so one would be out of its time: an anachronism.

items.q: Perennial contains per- (through) and enn (year). A perennial plant…
items.why: Per- + enn: through the years. A perennial comes back every year.

items.q: Type the word that means arranged in the order in which things happened.
